findings.description: storage_encrypted is explicitly set to false, so the RDS MySQL instance's underlying storage, snapshots and backups are stored unencrypted with no KMS customer-managed key protection.
publicly_accessible = true assigns the database a public endpoint reachable from the internet, exposing the MySQL service well beyond the VPC and making it a direct target for credential attacks.

The master username is the default 'admin', a predictable administrative account name that removes one unknown from brute-force or credential-stuffing attempts against the publicly reachable instance.

The master password is supplied through var.password, which is also interpolated into EC2 user data; the credential travels through Terraform state and plan output in plain text rather than being sourced from Secrets Manager or generated with managed master password support.

The instance user_data embeds the RDS master username and password (var.password) in a shell script; user data is retrievable by anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute or from the instance metadata service, leaking database credentials.

No metadata_options block is set, so the legacy instance metadata service (IMDSv1) remains available; a server-side request forgery in the PHP application on this host could be used to retrieve the instance profile's credentials, which grant broad s3/ec2/rds access.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the instance's root volume — which stores the plaintext dbinfo.inc credentials file — may be created unencrypted.

The inline role policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*", giving the EC2 instance effective administrative control over storage, compute and databases in the account; combined with reachable metadata this is a direct privilege-escalation path.
The rule allows all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0 from the database security group, providing an unrestricted data exfiltration and command-and-control channel.
